Who You Are and How You Already Lead

Leadership starts long before a title. In this module you will see leadership as influence you already use, put your identity and values into words, and take an honest baseline of your skills, blind spots, barriers and support so you know exactly where to start.
Leadership as influence: from the household to public life
Explain the difference between leadership as a position and leadership as influence
Name the four spheres where women lead, from household to civic life
Identify the five practices leaders carry out in any group
Recognise leadership you already practise but have not called by that name

Ask ten people to describe a leader and most will describe a person with a title: a chairman, a pastor, a governor, a manager. Titles matter, but they are not the whole story. In this course, **leadership means influencing people to work together toward a shared goal**. A title can give you authority, but influence comes from what you do: how you organise, decide, listen and keep your word.

This matters because many women already lead without being called leaders. The woman who keeps the records of an ajo or esusu savings group, the one who settles quarrels in the compound, the one the market women send to speak to the local government officer: each of them is influencing people toward a goal. Naming this is the first step to doing it on purpose and doing it better.
Three ideas people often mix up
Idea
What it means
What it looks like
Position
A formal role given by election, appointment or inheritance
Treasurer of the women's fellowship, CDA secretary, ward councillor
Influence
People choose to follow your lead because they trust you
Neighbours ask your advice before deciding where to send children to school
Service
Using your role or influence for the good of the group, not only yourself
Publishing the group's accounts every month so everyone can see where money went

The strongest leaders combine all three: they hold a position when it is useful, they earn influence through consistent behaviour, and they use both to serve. A person with a position but no influence is obeyed only when watched. A person with influence but no sense of service can lead people in the wrong direction.
The four spheres where women lead
Spheres of leadership
Civic and public life
Community and estate
Groups and associations
Household and family
Most women build leadership habits in the wider base spheres first, then carry them upward into community and civic roles.
**Household and family:** budgeting, planning children's education, deciding how to care for an elderly parent, resolving conflict between relatives.
**Groups and associations:** savings groups, cooperative societies, religious women's groups, market associations, alumni and town unions.
**Community and estate:** the Community Development Association (CDA), landlord and tenant associations, sanitation days, security arrangements, school parent-teacher associations.
**Civic and public life:** ward and local government meetings, elections, public hearings, advocacy to officials, boards of NGOs.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 5 includes target 5.5: "Ensure women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making in political, economic and public life." This course is built around that target. It is also realistic: target 5.4 of the same goal recognises the heavy load of unpaid care and domestic work, which is one reason women's time for leadership is limited. We will plan around that, not ignore it.
Five things leaders actually do
**Set direction:** help the group agree what it is trying to achieve.
**Organise:** turn the goal into tasks, people and resources (money, time, tools).
**Decide:** make or guide decisions, especially when people disagree.
**Communicate:** keep everyone informed, listen, and explain the reasons behind decisions.
**Follow through:** keep promises, check progress and take responsibility when things go wrong.
Worked example: spotting leadership you already practise

Ngozi, for example, sells foodstuff in a market in Onitsha. She has run a 10-member ajo savings group for two years. Each member contributes ₦5,000 every week and one member collects the whole pot in turn.
She works out the pot: 10 members × ₦5,000 = ₦50,000 collected each week, so one full cycle takes 10 weeks and every member receives ₦50,000 once.
She lists what she actually does each week: collects contributions, writes them in a notebook, reminds late payers on WhatsApp, and pays out the pot.
When two members argued about who should collect first, she suggested drawing lots in front of everyone and the group agreed.

She matches her tasks to the five practices: direction (the group's savings purpose), organising (collection and records), deciding (drawing lots), communicating (reminders), follow-through (paying out on time for two years).

Ngozi practises all five leadership behaviours every week. She is not starting from zero: she is starting from experience she had never named. Her next step is to use the same habits in a wider sphere, such as her market association.
Leadership is not dominance

Talking loudest, controlling money or making every decision alone is not strong leadership. It usually produces silent resentment and weak follow-through. Influence that lasts comes from fairness, clear communication and keeping your word.
A group of women standing together and celebrating
Leadership in this course is something women practise together in households, groups and communities, not only on a podium.

Over the next eight lessons you will move from understanding to action: first you will clarify your identity, values and starting point, then practise the tools of group leadership, and finally plan and carry out a small, real contribution to your community, with evidence you can show.

Identity and values: knowing what you stand for
Draw an identity map showing your roles, groups, values and story
Narrow a long list of values to your top three and define each as a behaviour
Explain how imposed "single stories" can limit how women see themselves
Write a three-sentence story of self you can use when introducing yourself as a leader

Your **identity** is the set of answers to the question "Who am I?" It includes the roles you hold (mother, trader, nurse, daughter-in-law), the groups you belong to (your ethnic group, faith community, town union, profession), the values you try to live by, and the story you tell about your life. Most women hold many identities at once. That is not confusion; it is a resource. Each identity connects you to different people and gives you different knowledge.

Identity matters for leadership because people follow those they understand and trust. When you know what you stand for, your decisions become more consistent, and consistency is what turns a single good act into a reputation.
Your identity map
**Roles:** what you do for others at home, at work and in the community.
**Groups:** the communities you belong to by birth, faith, work or choice.
**Values:** the principles that guide your choices when no one is checking.
**Story:** the key experiences that shaped you, including hardships you came through.
From values to influence
Know your values
Choose by them
Act consistently
Earn trust
Gain influence
Values only build influence when they show up repeatedly in your choices, so people learn they can rely on you.
Finding your top three values
Write down 15 values that feel important, for example honesty, fairness, faith, family, hard work, independence, generosity, respect, courage, learning, excellence, peace, justice, loyalty, service.
Cross out until only 5 remain. Ask: if I had to give this one up to keep the others, could I?
Cross out two more so you have your top 3.
For each value, finish the sentence "I show this when I..." with something you actually do, not something you wish you did.
Test them: recall a hard decision from the past year. Did these values guide you? If a different value really decided it, consider swapping it in.
Worked example: turning values into behaviours
Amaka, for example, is a nurse in Enugu who also leads the welfare committee of her church women's group. She does the values sort one evening after work.
She starts with 15 values and narrows to 5: honesty, fairness, family, faith and service.
She narrows to 3: honesty, fairness and service.

She writes behaviours: honesty, "I show this when I read out the welfare fund balance at every meeting"; fairness, "I show this when I use the same rule for every member who asks for support"; service, "I show this when I visit sick members myself, not only send messages".
She tests them: last month a member offered her ₦20,000 to approve her request ahead of two older requests. Amaka refused and kept the order of the list.

Amaka now has three values she can name and point to in action. When committee members disagree, she can explain her position by her values ("we use one rule for everyone"), which makes her decisions easier to accept.
When values pull in different directions

Values sometimes clash, for example family and service when a community task falls on your child's exam week. Decide which value leads in that specific situation, give the other a fixed time later, and tell people honestly. Clear priorities are better than half-doing both.
The danger of a single story

Other people also tell stories about who you are: "women from that area don't speak in public", "a widow should keep quiet", "she only has secondary school education". The Nigerian writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie describes how a single story repeated often enough becomes the only story people see. Leadership includes refusing to let one narrow story define you or the women around you.
Your story of self

The organiser and teacher Marshall Ganz uses the idea of a "story of self": a short account of why you care, rooted in a real experience, so that others understand what moves you to act. You will use yours in meetings, when asking for support and when introducing a community project. Keep it to three sentences: where you come from, a moment that made you care, and what you are doing about it now.
**Where I come from:** "I grew up in Aba, the eldest of five, and helped my mother sell provisions after school."
**A moment that made me care:** "When our street flooded in 2019, I watched traders lose a week of stock while everyone waited for someone else to act."
**What I am doing now:** "So I organise our monthly gutter clearing and I am learning to bring more women into our CDA's decisions."
**Check it:** is it true, short enough to say in under a minute, and does it show a value in action rather than just naming it?
Many identities, many bridges

Each identity you hold connects you to a different group. A Muslim trader who is also a member of a mixed town union can carry ideas between groups that rarely meet. Leaders who notice these bridges can bring people together who would otherwise never cooperate.
A compass
Your top three values work like a compass: they do not tell you every step, but they keep you pointed in a consistent direction.
Identity includes your roles, groups, values and story; having many identities is a strength.
Narrow your values to three and define each as something you actually do.
Consistency between values and actions is what builds trust and influence.
Do not let a single story told about you set the limit of what you can do.

Write 15 values on paper or in your phone notes and narrow them to 5, then to 3.
For each of the 3, write one "I show this when I..." sentence from real life.
Write a three-sentence story of self: where you come from, a moment that made you care, what you are doing now.
Read your story aloud twice, or record it as a WhatsApp voice note to yourself and listen back.

A baseline is a measurement taken at the start so that you can see change later. Without one, growth is easy to forget and setbacks feel bigger than they are. In this lesson you will rate your skills, ask for outside views, name your barriers honestly and choose a single focus.
Rate six core skills
Give yourself a score from 1 (rarely) to 5 (consistently) for each skill. Score what you do now, not what you hope to do.
Skill

Shares views clearly and briefly when it matters

Can repeat back others' points so they feel heard
Deciding
Delays or leaves decisions to others
Weighs options against values and decides in time
Handling disagreement
Avoids it or becomes angry

Worked example: reading a baseline
Halima, for example, runs a tailoring shop in Kaduna and attends her area's women's association. She completes the self-rating on her phone.
Her scores: speaking up 2, listening 4, deciding 3, handling disagreement 2, organising 4, following through 5.
Total: 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 20 out of a possible 30. Average: 20 ÷ 6 = about 3.3.
Her strengths (4 and above): listening, organising and following through.
Her two lowest scores are speaking up and handling disagreement. She notices they are linked: she keeps quiet partly to avoid arguments.
She chooses one focus: speaking up in her women's association meetings.
Halima has a clear starting point (20 out of 30) and one specific skill to practise. In Module 2 she will track how often she speaks up and compare it with this baseline.
Finding blind spots: the Johari window
The Johari window
Open: known to me and others
Blind spot: others see, I don't
Hidden: I know, others don't
Unknown: no one sees yet
Known to me, then not known to me
Known to others, then not known to others
Feedback shrinks your blind spot and careful sharing shrinks your hidden area, so the open area where trust grows becomes larger.

The Johari window, created by psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham, divides what can be known about you into four areas. Your **blind spot** holds things others notice but you do not, for example that you sound impatient when tired, or that people trust you more than you think. The only way to see it is to ask. Choose two people who want good for you and ask: "What is one thing I do well when working with people, and one thing I could do better?" Write down the answers without arguing.
Ask by private message or face to face, not in a group chat, so people feel free to be honest.
Tell them why: "I am working on my leadership and I value your view."
Accept what they say with a simple thank you, even if it surprises you.
Look for patterns: if two people mention the same thing, treat it as a real blind spot.
Do the same exercise again at the end of the course and compare the answers.

Your **hidden** area also matters. Some things you keep private for good reasons, but sharing a relevant experience, for example that you once struggled to pay school fees, can make people trust your leadership on that issue. Share deliberately, not by accident.
Naming barriers honestly
**Time:** cooking, childcare and caring for relatives take hours each day. Response: choose roles with fixed, limited hours and negotiate shared tasks at home.
**Social expectations:** some people disapprove of women speaking in mixed meetings. Response: start where women's voices are accepted, build allies, and let results speak.
**Self-doubt:** the inner voice that says "who am I to talk?" Response: rely on your evidence (your leadership map and baseline), not your feelings alone.
**Money and transport:** meetings cost fares and data. Response: ask for meetings at accessible times and places, or join by phone or WhatsApp.
**Safety:** late evening meetings or travel alone can be risky. Response: meet in daylight, in public places, and travel with someone.
Pick one context and one skill
Trying to grow everywhere at once leads to exhaustion. Choose one context (household, a group, the community or civic life) and one skill from your baseline. You will practise it throughout Module 2.
Your support system

Leadership grows faster with three kinds of support: a **mentor** who gives advice from experience, **peers** who are growing alongside you, and a **sponsor**, a person with influence who mentions your name when opportunities come up. Write the names you already have. Empty boxes are not failure; they are a task for Module 3.

Leadership Practice: Meetings, Inclusion and Tracking Growth

This module gives you the working tools of group leadership. You will learn to run a meeting that ends in a clear decision, lead in a way that includes everyone and keeps people and money safe, and keep a simple log that shows your leadership growing week by week.
Running a meeting that reaches a clear decision
Prepare an agenda and assign the chair, secretary and timekeeper roles
Lead a meeting through the standard order from opening to next date
Choose between consensus, majority vote, consult-then-decide and delegation
Record decisions as minutes with who does what by when

Much of community leadership happens in meetings: the women's association, the cooperative, the CDA, the parent-teacher association. Poorly run meetings drag on, end without a decision and leave people grumbling afterwards. Well run meetings are short, fair and end with clear actions. This is a skill you can learn step by step.
Before the meeting
**Purpose:** write in one sentence what the meeting must achieve, for example "agree how members will pay for the new canopy".
**Agenda:** a short numbered list of items, shared at least two days ahead on the group's WhatsApp, so people come prepared.
**Roles:** the **chair** guides discussion and keeps order; the **secretary** records decisions; the **timekeeper** watches the clock.
**Quorum:** check your group's constitution or rules for the minimum number of members needed for decisions to count.
**Time and place:** choose a time women can attend, for example after market hours, and a safe, accessible venue.
The order of a meeting
Meeting flow
Open and confirm quorum
Adopt last minutes
Discuss each item
Decide and record
Assign actions
Fix next date
Following the same order every time makes meetings predictable, fair and much shorter.

Open with the customary greeting or prayer, then confirm that quorum is present. Read the minutes of the last meeting and ask a member to move that they are adopted as a true record. Review "matters arising", meaning actions from last time. Take each agenda item in turn: the chair introduces it, invites views, summarises, then moves to a decision. End with any other business, the date of the next meeting and a close.

How it works
Best for
Watch out for
Consensus

Can take long; a few people can block
Majority vote
The option with more than half of the votes cast wins
Larger groups, clear choices
The losing side may feel left out; explain and include them
Consult then decide
Leader hears views, then decides and explains why
Urgent or technical issues
Only works if people trust the leader
Delegate
Group hands the decision to a person or committee
Detailed tasks such as choosing a supplier
Set limits, for example a maximum amount to spend
Worked example: deciding a levy fairly

A market women's association in Ibadan has 40 members. For example, its rules say quorum is half the members. The members want a new canopy. The quote is about ₦360,000 (an approximate price; get your own quotes).
Agenda shared on WhatsApp three days ahead: item 2 is "How to pay for the canopy".
On the day 26 members attend. Quorum is 40 ÷ 2 = 20, and 26 is more than 20, so decisions are valid.
The treasurer presents two options. Option A: a one-off levy of ₦360,000 ÷ 40 = ₦9,000 per member. Option B: the same ₦9,000 paid as ₦3,000 per month for 3 months.
After discussion the chair calls a vote. 17 vote for B, 6 for A, 3 abstain. Votes cast: 17 + 6 = 23; more than half of 23 is 12 or more, and 17 is more than 12, so B wins.
The secretary records: decision B; treasurer to collect ₦3,000 per member monthly, issue receipts and report the balance at each meeting; canopy ordered once ₦360,000 is in the account.

The meeting ends with one clear decision, a fair payment plan, a named person responsible and a way for every member to check the money. Absent members can read the minutes on WhatsApp and know exactly what to pay.
Minutes that people actually use

Good minutes are short. For each item record only the decision, the person responsible and the deadline. Share them within 48 hours so memories are fresh and disagreements about what was agreed are settled quickly.
Chairing skills for difficult moments
**Someone dominates:** thank them, summarise their point in one sentence, then say "Let us hear from those who have not spoken yet."
**Discussion goes in circles:** summarise the options on the table and ask "Are we ready to decide, or is there new information?"
**An off-topic issue comes up:** write it down as "parked" and promise a time to discuss it, under any other business or at the next meeting.
**Tempers rise:** call a five-minute break, speak to the people involved separately, then return to the facts.
Start with why

People commit more readily when they understand the purpose, not only the task. Before asking a group to contribute money or time, explain why it matters to them: "We lose sales every rainy season because customers avoid our wet stalls" is more persuasive than "We need a canopy". Simon Sinek's well-known talk explains this idea of starting with why.
People seated around a table in a meeting
A clear agenda, fixed roles and recorded decisions turn a long talk into a meeting that gets things done.
Share a short agenda ahead and assign chair, secretary and timekeeper.
Confirm quorum before making decisions that bind the group.
Pick the decision method that fits the group and the issue.
Record each decision with a person responsible and a deadline, and share minutes within 48 hours.

Choose a real meeting you will attend or lead in the next two weeks.
Write a one-sentence purpose and a numbered agenda of no more than five items.
Note which decision method fits the main item and why.
After the meeting, write minutes for one item: decision, person responsible, deadline.

Inclusive, safe and sustainable leadership
Identify who is often left out of community decisions and why
Apply at least four techniques that bring quiet and excluded voices in
Follow basic safeguarding, money and data protection practices as a leader
Respond to public pushback calmly and turn it into a workable next step

A decision made by a few people for many people often fails, because those left out do not trust it, do not follow it, or were the ones who knew why it would not work. **Inclusive leadership** means everyone affected by a decision has a fair chance to be heard. It is not a favour; it produces better decisions.
Who is often left out
Women with disabilities, who may not reach upstairs or distant venues.
Older women and widows, whose views are sometimes dismissed.
Young women, who may be told to wait their turn.
Women who cannot read, when decisions are shared only in writing.
Newcomers or women who speak a different first language.
Women working at the meeting time, such as traders or shift workers.
Techniques that widen the circle
**Go round the room:** give every person a short turn before open discussion, so quieter members speak before the loudest set the direction.
**Small groups first:** split into groups of four or five to discuss, then each group reports back.
**Choose access:** ground-floor venues, times after market hours, and a phone or WhatsApp option for those who cannot travel.
**Use shared languages:** allow contributions in Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba or another local language and arrange someone to interpret.
**Read decisions aloud:** never rely only on written notices.
**Collect private input:** a suggestion box or private WhatsApp messages for people who will not speak in public.
Inclusion check before any meeting
Suitable time and place
Accessible venue
Language everyone understands
Every voice invited
Decisions read back aloud
Running through this short checklist before each meeting catches most of the reasons people end up excluded.
Keeping people, money and information safe

Leaders carry a duty of care. **Safeguarding** means protecting people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm during activities you organise. Practical habits: never leave a child alone with one adult behind a closed door during group activities; ask permission before taking or posting anyone's photo, and a parent's permission for children; and know where to refer someone who discloses abuse, such as a trusted health facility, the police or a recognised support organisation in your state.
Group money and personal data

Use a group bank account with at least two signatories, issue receipts for every payment, and report balances at every meeting. Never share members' phone numbers, addresses or ID details outside the group without their consent: Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data. Beware of scams that ask leaders to pay a fee to receive a grant; genuine funders do not charge to release money.
When someone pushes back in public
Worked example: turning pushback into a trial
Fatima, for example, lives in an estate in Kano. At a CDA meeting she proposes that women have a seat on the executive committee. An elder objects loudly that this is not how things have been done.
She lets him finish without interrupting, then summarises his point: "You are concerned that changing the committee could cause division."
She connects to a shared goal: "We all want the estate safe and clean, and women run most of the sanitation work."
She proposes a small, time-limited step: one women's representative, attending executive meetings for 6 months, then a review.
Before the next meeting she visits two respected members privately to explain the proposal and ask for support.
At the next meeting the trial is approved by vote, with the review date written in the minutes.
Instead of a public fight, Fatima secured a concrete trial with a review date. The elder's concern was heard, and the women gained a real voice that can be judged on results.

Pushback is common when women step into visible roles. Treat it as information: what is the person actually worried about? Respond to the worry, keep your tone calm, and offer a small, reversible step. Allies who speak for you are often more persuasive than speaking for yourself. If pushback turns into threats or harassment, put your safety first, document what happened and seek help from trusted leaders.
Leading without burning out

A leader who takes every task ends up exhausted and leaves the group dependent on her. Limit yourself to one or two roles at a time, share tasks with named people and dates, and rest without guilt. Training someone else to do part of your job is itself an act of leadership.

When you delegate, be specific: name the task, the person, the deadline, the resources available and how they should report back. "Kemi, please collect quotes for chairs from three shops by Friday and post them on the group" works far better than "someone should look into chairs". Check in once halfway, then let the person do it their way.
A small group of people standing together
Inclusive leadership brings everyone affected into the circle, which makes decisions stronger and easier to carry out.
Inclusive decisions are better decisions because more knowledge and trust go into them.
Go-round turns, small groups, accessible venues and shared languages bring excluded voices in.

Answer pushback by naming the worry, linking to a shared goal and offering a small trial.

Write in your notebook or a phone notes app. Keep it honest: record the times you stayed silent too, with what stopped you. Those entries are just as useful because they show you what to practise.
**Situation:** where it happened and who was there, in a few words.
**Skill:** the one skill from your baseline that the moment called for.
**What I did:** your actual words or actions, not your intentions.
**Result:** what happened next, including how people responded.
**Next time:** one small change you will try, so every entry ends with a lesson.
Make logging a habit
Attach logging to something you already do weekly, such as Sunday evening or the day you restock your shop. A WhatsApp chat with only yourself, or a voice note, works well if writing is slow for you.
Worked example: comparing four weeks against a baseline
Halima, for example, chose speaking up as her focus with a baseline score of 2. She counts every time she shared a view in a group setting.
Week 1: 1 time. Week 2: 2 times. Week 3: 2 times. Week 4: 4 times.
Total: 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9 times in four weeks. Average: 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 times a week.
From week 1 to week 4 the count went from 1 to 4, four times as often.
Two of her suggestions were adopted by the group and one was rejected; she notes what made the adopted ones work (she prepared them in writing first).
She re-rates speaking up at the end of week 4: 3 out of 5, up from 2.
Halima has clear evidence of growth: a rising count, two adopted suggestions and a one-point rise on her self-rating. She keeps the same focus for another month and aims for at least 3 times a week.
Getting feedback: Stop, Start, Continue
Choose one or two people who saw you in action, such as a fellow group member.
Ask three short questions: what should I stop doing, start doing and continue doing when I lead?
Listen and write the answers without defending yourself; say thank you.
Pick one point to act on and record it in your log.
Measuring what you do for the community
Outputs and outcomes
Outputs: what we did
Outcomes: what changed
3 sanitation days held
25 households took part
1 letter sent to councillor
Street no longer floods after rain
Refuse collected weekly
More women attend CDA meetings
Outputs show effort; outcomes show whether life actually improved, so track both.

**Outputs** are the activities you carried out and are easy to count. **Outcomes** are the changes that result, and they take longer. A good tracker records both: "We held three clearing days (output) and the street did not flood in the next two heavy rains (outcome)." You will use this when planning your community project in Module 3.
Choosing simple indicators

An **indicator** is a sign you can count or observe that tells you whether things are changing. Good indicators are few, easy to collect and linked to your goal. For personal growth, count the behaviour you are practising. For a community activity, pick one output and one outcome indicator and note them on the same day each month.

Never inflate your numbers

Report what really happened, including small numbers and failures. Exaggerated results destroy trust when people check, and funders and officials often do. An honest "12 people came, fewer than we hoped" is far stronger than a doubtful "over 100 people".

A cooperative has 30 members and its rules set quorum at half the members. 14 members arrive. What should the chair do?
Hold the vote; most of those present agree
Discuss the items but postpone binding decisions until quorum is met
Ask the 14 to vote on behalf of the absent members
Cancel the cooperative's plans
Quorum is 30 ÷ 2 = 15. With 14 present, decisions would not be valid, so binding decisions should wait.
In a vote, 11 members choose option A, 9 choose option B and 4 abstain. Under simple majority of votes cast, what is the result?
No decision, because 11 is less than half of 24
Option B wins
Option A wins, because 11 is more than half of the 20 votes cast
The chair must decide
Votes cast are 11 + 9 = 20. More than half of 20 is 11 or more, so option A passes.
Which minutes entry is most useful?
"Long discussion about the canopy"
"Members were happy"
"Canopy to be discussed further"
"Treasurer to collect ₦3,000 per member monthly from April, report at each meeting"
Good minutes record the decision, the person responsible and the deadline, so everyone knows what happens next.
During a meeting, the same three women do all the talking while others stay silent. What is the best next step for the chair?
Go round the room and give each person a short turn
End the meeting early
Ask the quiet women why they never contribute
Let the three women decide since they are most interested
A go-round gives every member a turn before open discussion, so quieter voices are heard without being singled out.
Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?
Three sanitation days were held
40 flyers were shared on WhatsApp
The street did not flood after the next two heavy rains
One letter was sent to the councillor
Outputs are activities carried out; an outcome is a change in conditions, such as the street no longer flooding.
Someone messages the women's group treasurer saying a grant of ₦2 million is approved but she must first pay a ₦50,000 processing fee. What should she do?
Pay quickly so the group does not lose the grant
Pay half and ask for the rest later
Treat it as a likely scam, pay nothing and verify with the funder through official contacts
Share members' bank details so the funder can pay them directly
Genuine funders do not charge fees to release grants. She should pay nothing, protect members' data and verify independently.
Community Development in Action

Now you put leadership to work for your community. You will find a real need and the assets already present, plan a small, affordable project, bring the right stakeholders and mentors on board, and finish with a portfolio and a 90-day plan that keeps you growing.
From need to action: planning a small community project
Gather information on a community need using a walk, conversations and records
Map community assets using the six categories of asset-based community development
Separate a problem's root causes from its effects with a problem tree
Write a SMART project goal with a simple, fully costed budget

**Community development** means people working together to improve conditions in their own community, using their own knowledge and resources first and outside help second. Your project does not need to be large. A well run small project that people can see and trust is the best foundation for bigger ones.

A useful approach is **Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD)**, associated with John McKnight and John Kretzmann. Instead of starting with a list of what the community lacks, it starts by mapping what the community already has. People who are only described by their needs tend to wait for rescue; people who see their assets start acting.
Step 1: Listen and look
**Community walk:** walk the area with two or three others and note problems and resources you see (blocked drains, an empty hall, a busy borehole).
**Conversations:** ask at least 10 people from different groups the same two questions: what would make life here better, and what are you willing to do about it?
**Existing information:** check notices, CDA records, the school or primary health centre, which may already know key facts.
**Community meeting:** share what you found and let people choose priorities.
Step 2: Map your assets
Asset type
Examples in a Nigerian community
Individuals
A retired teacher, a woman who keeps excellent records, youths with phones and data
Associations
Women's fellowship, market association, town union, age grades, cooperatives
Institutions
Schools, primary health centre, mosque or church, local government offices
Physical assets
Community hall, open land, boreholes, roads, shops
Economic assets
Local businesses, savings groups, market days
Culture and stories
Festivals, shared history, traditions of communal work
Step 3: Find the root cause

A **problem tree** helps you avoid solving the wrong problem. Write the main problem in the middle (the trunk). Below it, write the causes (the roots): ask "why does this happen?" several times. Above it, write the effects (the branches): what happens because of the problem. Then choose a root cause that your group can actually act on. Fixing a root cause solves the problem for longer; treating only an effect means you will be back next season facing the same trouble.
Small project cycle
Listen and look
Map assets
Choose one root cause
Plan with SMART goal
Act together
Review and share results
Each step builds on the one before, and sharing results at the end builds trust for the next project.
Worked example: planning a drainage clearing project

Chioma, for example, lives on a street in Port Harcourt with 30 households. Every rainy season the street floods and some shops close. On the community walk her team finds the main gutter blocked with refuse and sand.
Problem tree: problem is flooding; root causes are refuse dumped in the gutter and no regular clearing; effects are lost sales, damaged goods and stagnant water that breeds mosquitoes.
Assets: 12 residents willing to work one Saturday a month, a church compound to store tools, a resident with a pickup who will carry waste to the approved dumpsite.

Budget (approximate prices, check your own market): 3 shovels at ₦7,500 = ₦22,500; 2 rakes at ₦4,000 = ₦8,000; 20 pairs of heavy gloves at ₦1,000 = ₦20,000. Total: ₦22,500 + ₦8,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦50,500.
Contribution: ₦50,500 ÷ 30 households = about ₦1,683, rounded up to ₦1,700. Collected: 30 × ₦1,700 = ₦51,000, leaving ₦500 kept as a recorded balance.
SMART goal: "By the end of June, residents will clear the main gutter on the first Saturday of every month, so that the street does not flood after heavy rain."
Chioma's team has a cheap, specific project based on a root cause, funded by the community itself, with every naira accounted for. It is small enough to succeed and visible enough to build trust.
Working safely on clean-ups

Wear gloves and closed shoes or boots, never handle broken glass or sharp metal with bare hands, keep children away from the work, do not enter fast-flowing water, and wash hands with soap and clean water afterwards. Take waste to an approved dumpsite and never into a river or canal.
A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Test yours: could a neighbour tell, on a fixed date, whether it was achieved? If not, make it more specific.
Choosing a first project wisely
**Felt need:** many people, not only you, named it in the conversations.
**Within your control:** the group can act mostly with its own time, skills and money.
**Affordable:** the cost per household or member is small enough that most can pay.
**Visible:** people will see the result, which builds trust for the next project.
**Safe and lawful:** it needs no risky work and does not break local rules; check with the CDA or LGA if unsure.

Stakeholders, partners and mentors: building support for your project
Name the local stakeholders who can help or block a community project
Place stakeholders on a power and interest grid and decide how to engage each
Write a short, specific request letter to an official or organisation
Find a mentor and peers and offer support to another woman in return

No community project succeeds on one person's energy. A **stakeholder** is anyone who affects or is affected by your project. Some can give permission, money or labour; some can block you if they feel ignored. Leading well means knowing who they are and talking to the right people at the right time.

Respect local protocol. In many communities, visiting the traditional or community head before a public activity is expected courtesy, and skipping it can turn a supporter into an opponent. Ask an older member how things are usually done, and go with one or two others rather than alone so the visit represents the group, not just you.
Who's who in your community
**Traditional and community heads:** the Baale, Obi, Emir's representative or village head, whose blessing often opens doors.
**Community Development Association (CDA) and landlords' associations:** organise residents and often run sanitation and security.
**Elected officials:** your ward councillor and the Local Government Area (LGA) chairman's office, which manage local services such as waste collection.
**Religious bodies:** churches and mosques with halls, members and trust.
**Schools and primary health centres:** institutions with staff and information.
**NGOs and community-based organisations (CBOs):** may offer training, materials or small grants.
**Women's groups and market associations:** your natural allies and labour force.
Mapping power and interest
Stakeholder power and interest grid
Keep satisfied
Work closely with
Monitor
Keep informed
Interest: low to high
Power: high to low
Spend most effort on high-power, high-interest stakeholders, while keeping powerful but less interested people satisfied and supporters informed.

The grid places each stakeholder by **power** (how much they can help or block you) and **interest** (how much they care about this project). High power and high interest: work closely, involve them in planning. High power, low interest: keep them satisfied with short, respectful updates. Low power, high interest: keep them informed; they are often your most loyal volunteers. Low power, low interest: monitor and share results publicly.
Worked example: placing stakeholders for the drainage project
Chioma's street project, for example, needs regular refuse pickup so the gutter stays clear after each clearing day.
Ward councillor: high power, medium interest. Keep satisfied: send a short letter and invite her to the first clearing day.
CDA chairman: high power, high interest. Work closely: present the plan at the CDA meeting and ask for it to be adopted as a CDA activity.
Shop owners on the street: lower power, high interest. Keep informed: weekly WhatsApp update with photos and the money balance.
Residents of the next street: low power, low interest for now. Monitor: share results publicly; they may want to copy the project.

Chioma knows where to spend her limited time. The CDA adopts the project, the councillor attends the first clearing day and arranges a refuse pickup, and shop owners contribute water and snacks for volunteers.
Asking well: the request letter
**Who we are:** one sentence naming your group and how many households or members it represents.
**What we have already done:** show your own effort first, for example "30 households contributed ₦51,000 and cleared the gutter on 1 June".
**The specific ask:** one clear request, such as weekly refuse collection from a named point.
**Why it matters:** the outcome you expect, such as no flooding and fewer mosquitoes.
**Contact and follow-up:** a name, phone number and the date you will follow up.
Transparency builds partners

Post a simple account after every activity on your group's WhatsApp: money in, money out, balance, with photos of receipts. Officials and NGOs are far more willing to support groups that already show honest records.

Follow up on the date you promised, politely and briefly. If the answer is no, ask what would make a yes possible later, or who else could help. A refusal today often becomes support once the official sees your project working. Keep a simple record of every contact: who, when, what was asked and what was said.
The first follower

Movements often begin when one person acts and a second person publicly joins in. That first follower shows others it is safe to join. As a leader, welcome and honour your first followers by name; as a member, sometimes the bravest leadership is to be the first follower of another woman's good idea.
Mentors, peers and giving back

Approach a possible mentor with a specific request: "Could I ask you three questions about how you got the CDA to support women's projects, for 20 minutes next week?" Specific requests are easier to accept than "please mentor me". Join or form a peer circle of three to five women who meet monthly to share progress. And support another woman's growth now, even while you are still learning: reciprocity strengthens both of you.
Two hands in a handshake
Partnerships with officials, associations and mentors give a small project the reach and staying power one person cannot.

Use the power and interest grid to decide how much time each stakeholder gets.
Request letters work best when they show your own effort first and make one specific ask.

Your leadership and community impact portfolio and 90-day plan
Write a structured reflection using What? So what? Now what?
Assemble evidence of a real household or community leadership contribution
Build a 90-day plan with monthly milestones for leadership and community impact
Plan how to hand over or sustain your project so it does not depend only on you

This lesson brings everything together into your capstone, the Leadership and Community Impact Project. It has three parts: a written reflection on your values, strengths and one leadership skill practised in a real situation; documentation of a specific household or community contribution; and a 90-day plan naming your next leadership goal and community step.
Part 1: Reflection with What? So what? Now what?

This three-question model, set out by Gary Rolfe and colleagues, keeps reflection practical. **What?** describes what happened. **So what?** explains what it means and what you learned, linked to your values and strengths. **Now what?** states what you will do differently next time. Aim for 300 to 500 words, written or recorded as a voice note and transcribed. Be honest about what did not go well: a reflection that admits a mistake and shows what you learned is more convincing than one that only lists successes.
Worked example: a short reflection and plan
Halima, for example, focused on speaking up in her women's association in Kaduna and supported a market sanitation day.
What? "Over four weeks I spoke up 9 times. I proposed monthly dues instead of yearly dues and the association adopted it. I also organised 15 women for a sanitation day around our market section."

So what? "My values are fairness, service and hard work. Monthly dues are fairer for traders with small daily income. I learned that preparing my point in writing first makes me calm and clear. My blind spot, from feedback, was that I give up too quickly when someone disagrees."
Now what? "I will hold my point at least once more when challenged, and ask for a vote rather than dropping the idea."
Baseline comparison: speaking up rose from 2 to 3 out of 5; total baseline score rose from 20 to 22 out of 30.
Evidence attached: log pages, the minutes showing the dues decision, a group photo taken with consent and the sanitation day attendance list.
Halima's reflection is specific, linked to her values and backed by evidence. Anyone reading it can see what she did, what she learned and what she will do next.
Part 2: Documenting your contribution
**Minutes or notes** showing a decision you proposed or led.
**Attendance lists** with names and phone numbers kept private.
**Receipts and accounts** for any money handled.
**Before and after photos**, taken with permission, with no children's faces posted publicly without parental consent.
**Short statements** from one or two people who took part, in their own words.

90-day plan
Days 1 to 30: prepare
Days 31 to 60: act
Days 61 to 90: review
Day 90: share results
Breaking 90 days into three monthly phases makes progress easy to check and adjust.

Plan for handover from the start

A project that collapses when you are busy was never fully a community project. From month 1, name a deputy, share the records with two people, and write a one-page note on how the project runs. Training a successor is one of the clearest signs of mature leadership.

Keep your plan realistic for your time. If caring duties are heavy this quarter, choose fewer, smaller steps and complete them. Finished small steps build more confidence and trust than ambitious plans abandoned halfway.
Sharing results with the community

Reporting back is part of leadership, not an extra. At the end of your project or at day 90, give a short report at a meeting and on WhatsApp: what you set out to do, what was done (outputs), what changed (outcomes), the money in, money out and balance, who helped, and what comes next. Thank volunteers by name, and invite questions about the accounts openly rather than waiting for complaints. Keep the report under five minutes so people actually listen. People who see their effort recognised are far more likely to join the next activity.
**Common mistake:** a plan with ten goals. Keep one leadership goal and one community step per month.
**Common mistake:** no evidence collected until the end. Take notes and photos as you go.
**Common mistake:** money reported only when someone asks. Report balances every time.
**Common mistake:** doing it all yourself. Name a deputy in month 1.

What leadership means
Leadership starts long before a title
Leadership is influence toward a shared goal
A title is optional
Many women already lead without the name
Naming it lets you do it on purpose
In this course, leadership means influencing people to work together toward a shared goal.
A title can give you authority. But influence comes from what you do: how you organise, decide, listen and keep your word.
Think of the woman who keeps the records of an ajo savings group, or the one who settles quarrels in the compound. Each of them is leading.
Naming this is the first step to doing it on purpose, and doing it better.
Three ideas
Position, influence and service
A formal role by election, appointment or inheritance, like CDA secretary or ward councillor.
People choose to follow you because they trust you, like neighbours asking your advice.
Using your role for the good of the group, like publishing the group's accounts every month.
People often mix up three ideas. Position is a formal role, like treasurer of the women's fellowship.
Influence is when people choose to follow you because they trust you. A person with a position but no influence is obeyed only when watched.
Service is using your role and influence for the good of the group. The strongest leaders combine all three.
And remember, talking loudest or controlling money is not strong leadership. Lasting influence comes from fairness and keeping your word.
What leaders do
Five practices of every leader
Set direction: agree the goal
Organise: tasks, people, money, time
Decide, especially when people disagree
Communicate: inform, listen, explain
Follow through: keep promises
In any group, leaders do five things. They set direction, helping the group agree what it wants to achieve.
They organise, turning the goal into tasks, people and resources.
They decide, or guide decisions, especially when people disagree.
They communicate. They keep everyone informed, listen, and explain the reasons behind decisions.
And they follow through. They keep promises and take responsibility when things go wrong.
Worked example
Ngozi's ajo group
For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff in Onitsha and has run a 10-member ajo group for two years.
Each member pays every week
Pot collected each week
One full cycle takes 10 weeks.
Let us spot leadership Ngozi already practises. She runs a savings group of 10 members in an Onitsha market.
Each member contributes 5,000 naira every week.
So the pot is 50,000 naira each week, and every member collects it once in a 10 week cycle.
Each week Ngozi collects, records in a notebook, reminds late payers on WhatsApp and pays out. When two members argued about who should collect first, she suggested drawing lots in front of everyone.
That is all five practices, every week. She is not starting from zero. She is starting from experience she had never named.
Identity and values
Find your top three values
Write down 15 values that matter
Cross out until 5 remain
Cross out two more: your top 3
Finish: I show this when I...
Test them on a hard past decision
People follow those they understand and trust. So know what you stand for. Step one. Write 15 values, such as honesty, fairness, faith, family and service.
Step two. Cross out until 5 remain. Ask, could I give this one up to keep the others?
Step three. Cross out two more, so you have your top 3.

Step four. For each, finish the sentence, I show this when I, with something you actually do. For example, Amaka, a nurse in Enugu, wrote: I show fairness when I use the same rule for every member who asks for support.
Step five. Test them on a hard decision. When a member offered Amaka 20,000 naira to jump the queue, she refused and kept the order of the list.
Your baseline
Rate six skills from 1 to 5
Now take a baseline, a measurement at the start so you can see change later. Score each skill from 1, rarely, to 5, consistently. Score what you do now, not what you hope.
For example, Halima, a tailor in Kaduna, scored 20 out of 30. Speaking up and handling disagreement were lowest, so she chose one focus: speaking up in her women's association meetings.
Then ask two trusted people privately: what is one thing I do well with people, and one thing I could do better? That shows your blind spots.
Be honest
Real barriers, practical responses
Barrier
Time: cooking and childcare
Self-doubt: who am I to talk?
Fares and data for meetings
Late evening meetings
Response
Roles with fixed, limited hours
Rely on your evidence, not feelings
Join by phone or WhatsApp
Meet in daylight, travel with someone
Name your barriers honestly. Time, self-doubt, money for transport and safety are real.
Give each one practical response. Choose roles with fixed hours and share tasks at home. Lean on your leadership map and baseline when doubt speaks.
And for safety, meet in daylight, in public places, and travel with someone.
Key points
Remember
Leadership is influence; a title is optional
Every leader uses the same five practices
Define three values as real behaviours
Take a baseline and choose one focus skill

To remember. Leadership is influence, and a title is optional. Every leader uses the same five practices. Define your three values as things you actually do. And take a baseline, then pick one context and one skill to grow.

Run a meeting that decides, include everyone, and track your growth.
This is the video for Module 2 of Leadership, Identity, and Community Development.
Prepare so the meeting is short and fair
Purpose in one sentence
Short agenda, shared 2 days ahead
Roles: chair, secretary, timekeeper
Check quorum in your group's rules
A time and place women can attend

Poorly run meetings drag on and end without a decision. Good ones are short, fair and end with clear actions. Start by writing the purpose in one sentence, such as, agree how members will pay for the new canopy.
Share a short numbered agenda on WhatsApp at least two days ahead, so people come prepared.
Assign roles. The chair guides discussion, the secretary records decisions, and the timekeeper watches the clock.
Check quorum, the minimum number of members needed for decisions to count.
And choose a time women can attend, such as after market hours, in a safe, accessible venue.
Step by step
Record each decision: who does what, by when.
Adopt the last minutes
Discuss each item in turn
Fix the next date
Follow the same order every time. Open with the customary greeting or prayer, and confirm quorum.
Read the last minutes and adopt them, then check actions from last time.
Take each item in turn. The chair introduces it, invites views and summarises. If someone dominates, say, let us hear from those who have not spoken yet.
Then decide. Use consensus for small groups, a majority vote for clear choices, or delegate detailed tasks to a committee with limits.
Assign actions with names and deadlines, and fix the next date. Share short minutes within 48 hours.
Worked example
Paying for the market canopy
For example, a market women's association in Ibadan has 40 members and needs a new canopy.
Canopy quote
Option A: one-off levy each
Option B: per month, for 3 months
Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a fair decision in action. The rules say quorum is half the members. 26 of the 40 attend, which is more than 20, so decisions count.
The canopy quote is about 360,000 naira. Get your own quotes, as prices change.
Option A is a one-off levy. 360,000 divided by 40 is 9,000 naira per member.
Option B is the same 9,000 naira, paid as 3,000 naira a month for 3 months.
17 vote for B, 6 for A and 3 abstain. 17 is more than half of the 23 votes cast, so B wins.
The minutes say the treasurer collects monthly, issues receipts and reports the balance at every meeting.
Include everyone
A language everyone understands
A decision made by a few for many often fails. Women with disabilities, widows, young women, women who cannot read and traders working at meeting time are often left out.
So check the time, the venue and the language. Go round the room so quieter members speak first. And read decisions aloud, never only in writing.
Duty of care
Keep people, money and data safe
Never leave a child alone with one adult behind a closed door. Ask before posting anyone's photo.
A group account with at least two signatories, receipts for every payment, balances at every meeting.
Never share members' numbers, addresses or ID details outside the group without consent.
Leaders carry a duty of care. Safeguarding means protecting people, especially children, during your activities. Ask permission before posting anyone's photo, and a parent's permission for children.
Keep group money in an account with at least two signatories, and issue receipts. Beware of scams that ask leaders to pay a fee to receive a grant. Genuine funders do not charge to release money.
And never share members' phone numbers, addresses or ID details outside the group without their consent.
Track your growth
Outputs: we did
Outcomes: changed

Keep a five-minute weekly log: the situation, the skill, what you did, the result, and what you will try next time. For example, Halima counted how often she spoke up. It went from 1 time in week 1 to 4 times in week 4.
When you serve the community, track outputs too. These are what you did, and they are easy to count.
Outcomes are what actually changed, like a street that no longer floods. Track both, and never inflate your numbers. An honest 12 people came is stronger than a doubtful over 100.
Key points
Remember
Share the agenda ahead and assign roles
Confirm quorum before deciding
Bring quiet and excluded voices in
Two signatories, receipts, consent
Log weekly; track outputs and outcomes
To remember. Share the agenda ahead and assign roles. Confirm quorum. Bring quiet voices in. Protect people, money and data.
And keep a weekly log, so your growth becomes visible.

This is the video for Module 3 of Leadership, Identity, and Community Development.
Start with what you have
Community development, asset first
People improving their own community
Own knowledge and resources first
Outside help second
Small, visible and trusted beats large
Community development means people working together to improve conditions in their own community.

Asset-Based Community Development starts by mapping what the community already has, not only what it lacks. People described only by their needs tend to wait for rescue. People who see their assets start acting.
So use your own knowledge and resources first, and outside help second.
Your project does not need to be large. A small project people can see and trust is the best foundation for bigger ones.
Map your assets
Six kinds of community asset
Individuals: a retired teacher, a record keeper
Associations: fellowship, market group, age grades
Institutions: schools, health centre, worship
Physical: hall, open land, boreholes
Economic: local businesses, savings groups
Culture: festivals, traditions of communal work

First, listen and look. Walk the area, ask at least 10 people what would make life better and what they are willing to do. Then map your assets. Individuals, like a retired teacher or youths with phones and data.
Associations, like the women's fellowship, the town union and cooperatives.
Institutions, like schools, the primary health centre and the mosque or church.
Physical assets, like a community hall or a borehole.
Economic assets, like savings groups and market days. And culture, like traditions of communal work.
Step by step
Problem tree to SMART goal
Fix a root cause, or you will be back next season.
Trunk: write the main problem
Roots: ask why it happens
Branches: write the effects
Choose one root cause you can act on
Write a SMART goal
For example, Chioma's street in Port Harcourt has 30 households and floods every rainy season. Flooding is the trunk of her problem tree.
Ask why, several times. The roots: refuse dumped in the gutter, and no regular clearing.
The branches are the effects: lost sales, damaged goods, and stagnant water that breeds mosquitoes.
Choose a root cause your group can act on. Treating only an effect means facing the same trouble next season.
Then write a goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Chioma's: by the end of June, residents will clear the main gutter on the first Saturday of every month.
Test it: could a neighbour tell, on a fixed date, whether it was achieved?
Worked example
Chioma's clearing budget
For example, Chioma's 30 households cost the tools for monthly gutter clearing.
3 shovels at 7,500
2 rakes at 4,000
20 pairs of heavy gloves at 1,000
Naira prices are approximate. Check your market.
Now cost it fully. 12 residents will work, a church compound will store the tools, and a neighbour with a pickup will carry waste to the approved dumpsite.
3 shovels at about 7,500 naira come to 22,500 naira.
2 rakes at 4,000 naira are 8,000 naira.
20 pairs of heavy gloves at 1,000 naira are 20,000 naira.
The total is 50,500 naira. Divided by 30 households, that is about 1,683 naira, rounded up to 1,700. They collect 51,000 naira and keep 500 naira as a recorded balance. Every naira is accounted for.
Safety first
Gloves and closed shoes or boots
No bare hands on glass or sharp metal
Keep children away from the work
Never enter fast-flowing water
Wash hands with soap afterwards
Waste to an approved dumpsite only
On clearing day, safety comes first. Wear gloves and closed shoes or boots. Never handle broken glass or sharp metal with bare hands. Keep children away, and do not enter fast-flowing water.
Wash with soap and clean water afterwards, and never dump waste into a river or canal.
Building support
A request letter in five parts
Show your own effort first, then make one clear ask.
Who we are
What we have already done
The one specific ask
Why it matters
Contact and follow-up date

Know your stakeholders: anyone who can help or block you. Visit the community head first, as local protocol expects. Work closely with high-power, high-interest people like the CDA chairman. Then write to officials in five parts. Start with who you are.
Show what you have already done. 30 households contributed 51,000 naira and cleared the gutter.
Make one specific ask, such as weekly refuse collection from a named point.
Say why it matters, then give a name, a phone number and the date you will follow up. And post your accounts after every activity. Officials support groups that keep honest records.
Your capstone
Reflect in three questions
What happened. Halima spoke up 9 times in four weeks and her monthly dues idea was adopted.
What it means, linked to your values. Preparing her point in writing made her calm and clear.
What you will do next. Hold her point once more when challenged, and ask for a vote.
Your capstone starts with a reflection in three questions. What happened? Halima spoke up 9 times in four weeks.
So what? What did it mean, and what did you learn? Be honest about what did not go well.
Now what? What will you do differently? Back it with evidence: minutes, receipts, attendance lists and photos taken with consent.
Key points
Remember
Map assets before needs
Act on a root cause you can reach
Cost it fully and report every naira
Show your effort, then make one ask
Name a deputy from month 1
To remember. Map assets first. Act on a root cause. Cost the project fully and report balances every time. Show your effort before you ask.
And name a deputy from month 1, so the project does not depend only on you.
